cards.title: Advertorial input-prep: strip the sales page into a clean text PDF once
cards.summary: Convert the sales page or sales letter you want advertorials for into an image-free PDF so it can be attached to AI prompts as the source of truth.
cards.use_when: You are about to produce advertorials (pre-sell articles) for a product page and need a reusable source document of the sales copy.
steps: Open the live landing page or sales letter you want advertorials to feed into.
Copy the main body copy, then paste into a Google Doc using paste-as-plain-text (Command/Ctrl+Shift+V) so styling and images don't come along.
Expand and copy the FAQ accordions — the presenter calls these valuable because objection answers are already written there.
Copy several testimonials (name plus quote) so the model has real social proof to reuse rather than inventing it.
Export the doc as PDF. This becomes the single attachment you re-use for every advertorial on that product.
Store the page URL at the top of the doc for reference.
Note that this prep is a one-time cost per product; all later advertorials reuse the same PDF.
caveats: Pasting without plain-text mode drags in HTML/images that break the AI attachment.
Short ecommerce pages will produce thin input — accept that and let the model fill gaps, then edit those gaps by hand.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Extract the sales-page input set before writing any advertorial
cards.summary: Run a fixed question battery against the sales-page PDF to pull target market, pain points, promises, proof, common failed solutions, real culprit, product facts and ingredients into one reusable doc.
cards.use_when: Product selection and messaging: you are preparing to write advertorials or ad angles and need the raw claims and audience material extracted first.
steps: Attach the image-free sales-page PDF and ask for: target market, market problems/pain points, and primary promises made.
Ask next for credible proof (universities, person's reference) and social proof (X number of people). If the page has none, note 'didn't have it for this page' and continue — don't stop the process.
Ask for common solutions mentioned in the sales letter plus why each isn't the real answer (e.g. strict keto, keto flu, exogenous ketones, fasting, excessive exercise).
Ask what the page names as the real culprit/mechanism, and the product description without naming the product, plus product name, how to consume, price and any exclusive price.
Ask for testimonials and for the ingredient list in a clean format.
Paste every output into one living 'inputs' document. This is what makes later advertorial runs fast and lets you skip re-analysis.
Correct anything the model invents if your brand page actually states the fact (e.g. real pricing).
caveats: On short ecommerce pages the model may say a section doesn't exist — that's expected; move on.
Treat extracted claims as raw material; you still own the accuracy check.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Split one broad product into avatar archetypes for advertorial variants
cards.summary: Ask the model to propose several audience archetypes from the extracted market data so each advertorial speaks to one specific segment instead of everyone.
cards.use_when: Product selection and creative strategy: you want multiple advertorial versions to test against different cold-traffic segments for the same product.
steps: After pulling target market and pain points, tell the model you'll write several advertorials and that speaking to everyone will underperform.

Ask it to propose avatar archetypes grounded only in the data you pulled, and state explicit constraints where you know the market (the presenter added: assume the market skews heavily female because the weight-loss market typically does).

Typical archetypes the model returned for a keto weight-loss product: busy working mom (20s–40s juggling work and family), post-pregnancy weight struggler (new mom 20s–late 30s), peri-menopausal woman (40s–50s, body change/fat gain/energy drop), yo-yo dieter, keto-conscious health enthusiast, post-retirement weight gainer.
Ask for more archetypes if you need more variants (the presenter asked for roughly 10).
For each archetype, write one parallel advertorial with matching demographic and psychographic experience.
Use the archetype list as your test matrix so creative variants differ by audience, not just by headline.
caveats: These archetypes are source-specific examples generated for one supplement, not a validated segmentation — validate against your own customer data.
Implied claims (menopause, post-pregnancy) need compliance review in many categories.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Find live advertorial swipe structures to model
cards.summary: Collect real advertorials from mainstream sites and spy tools to use as structural templates before writing.
cards.use_when: Creative strategy: you need proven advertorial structures to model your ecommerce advertorial on.
steps: Visit mainstream content sites — the presenter uses weather.com — and look in the sponsored content slots for advertorials.
Click a sponsored piece to see whether it leads to a long-form text advertorial or straight to a video sales letter (VSL).
Log which destination each uses; the presenter notes many advertisers go to advertorials, some go straight to VSL.
Also look in spy tools and simply browse sites you already read to spot advertorials in the wild.
Choose a swipe whose spokesperson type matches your brand's credibility (e.g. don't model a doctor-fronted advertorial if your brand has no doctor).
Feed one chosen swipe to the AI with the instruction to analyze its structure before writing anything new.
caveats: Swipe structures are templates for format and flow, not permission to copy claims, names or brand facts.
The presenter explicitly said he would not share one doctor-fronted swipe he used as a teaching example.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Advertorial architecture: the repeating section skeleton
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer the standard advertorial flow — problem story, failed solutions, discovery, mechanism, product reveal, proof, CTA — and reproduce it for your product.
cards.use_when: Landing-page and advertorial writing: you are drafting or reviewing an advertorial draft and need the structural spine it should follow.
steps: Identify the headline plus the subhead that functions as the reader's personal problem statement — the presenter maps 'my dog Daisy was slowing down, I was scared of losing her' to the 'I was drowning in mom guilt and stubborn baby weight' line.
Story: relatable protagonist with the avatar's problem and the daily life that makes it hard.
Failed solutions: list what the person tried (counting calories, intense workouts, hormone replacement therapy, strict keto/macros/meal prep) and why each failed.
Discovery: the article, expert or research that reframed the problem — ideally explains why the old approach was never going to work (e.g. even small amounts of carbs kick you out of ketosis).
Mechanism and product: name the supplement/drink and explain the blend that delivers the result plus how to consume it and the taste experience.
Proof: studies and testimonials, then a risk-free CTA and a link to the offer.
Write the advertorial section by section, telling the model to ask you to continue at each output limit rather than condensing, because effective direct response is usually longer.
caveats: The mechanism explanation is where hallucination risk is highest — verify any ingredient or biological claim before publishing.
Structure example comes from supplement advertorials; adapt section order for other categories.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Prompt pattern: model a new advertorial on a swipe plus your input doc
cards.summary: Combine an unrelated advertorial swipe, the extracted sales-page inputs and a chosen avatar into one prompt that produces a full draft in the swipe's style.
cards.use_when: PDP/landing-page work: you need a complete advertorial draft for a specific avatar written fast, in the style of a proven example.
steps: Attach the swipe advertorial and first ask the model to 'analyze the structure' — the presenter says this deliberate step primes the model on what an advertorial should look like.
Then instruct: write a new advertorial for [your product], follow the example advertorial page and its style and tone, base it on the sales page you reviewed, and match the named avatar archetype.
Add tone notes: match the example's sound, find a good blend of storytelling and news-article reporting.
Add a length note: take your time, go section by section, ask me to continue when you run out of space, and do not condense to conserve output.
If you're running the process a second time later, skip re-analysis and instead paste your saved input document plus the archetype into the prompt.
Review the output and correct placeholder specifics — real testimonials, real price, real flavor details — before it goes live.
caveats: The workflow assumes you keep the inputs document; without it you must re-run the extraction prompts.
Named experts, studies and testimonials produced by the model are often invented — the presenter flagged a doctor name it inserted that wasn't associated with the brand.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Scrub hallucinated spokespeople, studies and prices from AI drafts
cards.summary: Treat every named person, study citation, price and testimonial in an AI advertorial as unverified until checked against the real offer.
cards.use_when: Pre-publish QA on any AI-drafted advertorial or ad before it goes to the offer page.
steps: Flag any named doctor or expert. In the demo the model invented 'Dr Ryan Shelton'; the fix was to tell it to say the article came from 'an expert' or 'a world-renowned expert in holistic medicine and weight loss' without naming anyone.
If the real page has no doctor, tell the model not to use a doctor spokesperson at all and to leverage brand credibility or general experts instead.
Flag study citations — the model produced several 'clinical studies'; the presenter says you would want to look them up and make sure they're legit, and you can remove them entirely if not.
Flag prices and testimonials: the demo output did not match the actual page. If it's your brand you can fill in the true values up front; otherwise replace with real ones from the site.
Where your brand genuinely has studies (the presenter notes nutraceutical brands often do), you can supply them so the model doesn't fabricate.
Keep the advertorial clearly labeled as an advertisement/sponsored content at the top, as real advertorials do.
caveats: The presenter states plainly that hallucinations will occur, especially on short pages with little detail.
Regulatory exposure for health and weight-loss claims is high; this is editing guidance, not a compliance review.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Vary the swipe template as well as the avatar
cards.summary: Produce more advertorial variants by swapping the structural swipe (e.g. a doctor-fronted one) in addition to swapping the avatar.
cards.use_when: Creative testing at scale: you need a larger batch of distinct advertorial variants for one product to feed cold traffic.
steps: Hold the input document constant; change one variable at a time — avatar or swipe template.
For a second batch, attach a different advertorial example and repeat the analyze-structure step before writing.
Keep the same product and avatar to isolate the effect of format, or change avatar while holding format to isolate audience effect.
When the new swipe relies on credibility you don't have (a named doctor), substitute brand credibility or 'leading health and weight-loss experts' in the instructions.
The presenter produced three finished advertorials for one product in roughly 47 minutes including explanation, and estimates 5–10 per hour once the process is known.
Collect 10–20 advertorials produced this way as a test batch rather than shipping a single one.
caveats: Batch size is the presenter's own throughput estimate, not a performance benchmark; results depend on editing quality.
Don't model a format whose required assets (spokesperson type, video) you can't actually produce.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Advertorial as pre-sell between ad and offer
cards.summary: Use an advertorial when the destination page alone can't carry a cold reader, especially for short ecommerce pages or as a bridge to a long-form sales letter.
cards.use_when: Funnel architecture: deciding whether cold traffic should hit your ecommerce page directly or be routed through an advertorial first.
steps: Assess whether your page supplies enough information for a cold reader to buy. The presenter's example: sending a supplement buyer email straight to a short keto product page isn't enough information to sell, so it probably wouldn't convert well.
If the page is short-form ecommerce, slot an advertorial in front of it to do the pre-selling.
If you have a long-form sales letter, use the advertorial as an intermediary between the ad and the letter.
Understand that advertorials are structured as sponsored articles — the presenter calls them 'fake articles' labeled as ads — and have been used in direct response for about a century.
Keep the advertorial's labels and claims consistent with the destination page so the reader isn't surprised at the switch.
Route the advertorial CTA to either the ecommerce page or a video/long-form letter depending on where you intend to close.
caveats: The presenter's converting/not-converting statements are his expectation, not a measured benchmark.
Readers who feel tricked by an ad that reads as editorial can damage brand trust — label sponsorship clearly.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Keep a running outputs doc so later advertorial runs skip re-analysis
cards.summary: Persist the extracted inputs and each finished advertorial in a project document so future runs only need the swipe, the inputs and a new avatar.
cards.use_when: Landing-page production planning: you'll write advertorials for the same product repeatedly over weeks or months.
steps: Create a project doc holding the source page URL, the input-run outputs, and each finished advertorial labeled by number and avatar.
Also store alternative headline lists per advertorial — the presenter asked for extra headline options after each draft.
Save the swipe files you modeled on (or at least links), since each batch may use a different one.
When returning later, paste the inputs you previously pulled into the new prompt instead of re-attaching and re-analyzing the sales page.

Note which model/plan you used; the demo ran out of messages on Claude 3 and the presenter suggests a paid tier (~$20/month at the time) or switching models to keep writing. Verify the current interface and pricing before relying on this.
Format the final drafts for the destination (strip stray heading markers, set CTA links) before publishing.
caveats: Tool names, model versions, message limits and prices change — verify the current interface.
The presenter's paid-plan and pricing details were accurate only as of recording.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx
